newsitem.title: USA: Indiana tax seen triggering corn, soybean sales.
newsitem.headline: Indiana tax seen triggering corn, soybean sales.

text.p: Farmers scurrying to reduce their Indiana state inventory tax bill were expected to spur a wave of corn and soybean sales before the tax assessment deadline on March 1, merchandisers said.
"The inventory tax always helps facilitate grain movement," said one Indiana-based soybean merchandiser. "We always see more beans at tax time."
In an effort to reduce their tax liability by the March 1 assessment deadline, producers often sell some of their grain to Indiana elevators or nearby Illinois elevators, dealers said.

The inventory tax, which is part of the state's property tax, will add an estimated two cents per bushel on corn and and extra four to five cents per bushel on soybean inventories, said Bob Morgan, director of personal property for the Indiana State Board of Tax Commissioners.
The tax rate varies according to local tax districts, and one merchandiser estimated the soybean tax in his area would be as high as six cents per bushel.
The state inventory or property tax applies to all grain that is on the farm or in storage, and the person holding title to the grain is liable for the tax payment, Morgan said.
Alhtough most dealers expect an increase in sales in the coming weeks, one dealer said grain movement would increase only if road conditions in the state improved.
"I've seen a decline in movement recently, but it's only because the roads are so terrible," said Jim Quinton, merchandiser with Consolidated Grain and Barge in Mt. Vernon, Ind.
"If the roads improve, we should see Indiana bin doors flying open," he said.
Extremely cold weather followed by warmer weather is hard on secondary roads, and many states restrict hauling when that occurs
